reference.source: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies / WHO envenoming guidance
clinicalPearls: Reactions range from local swelling, through large local reactions, to systemic IgE-mediated anaphylaxis, which can be rapidly fatal
Anaphylaxis presents with urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, laryngeal oedema, hypotension and gastrointestinal symptoms, often within minutes
Intramuscular adrenaline is the first-line, life-saving treatment for anaphylaxis and should not be delayed for antihistamines or corticosteroids
Remove a retained bee stinger promptly; the method matters less than speed, as venom continues to be delivered while it remains
Massive envenomation from many simultaneous stings can cause a direct toxic reaction with haemolysis, rhabdomyolysis and organ injury, distinct from allergy
Biphasic reactions can occur, so a period of observation after apparent recovery is prudent
Patients with confirmed venom anaphylaxis should be referred for allergy assessment, prescribed an adrenaline auto-injector, and considered for venom immunotherapy
reference.pathophysiology: Hymenoptera venoms contain allergenic proteins (such as phospholipase and hyaluronidase) that, in sensitised individuals, cross-link IgE on mast cells and basophils, triggering degranulation and release of histamine and other mediators. This produces the vasodilatation, increased vascular permeability, bronchoconstriction and mucosal oedema of anaphylaxis, which can progress to airway obstruction and distributive shock. Separately, very large numbers of stings can cause a dose-dependent direct toxic syndrome from venom load, with haemolysis, rhabdomyolysis, hepatic and renal injury independent of allergic sensitisation.
additionalDifferentials: Anaphylaxis from another allergen (food, drug, latex)
Large local reaction or cellulitis at the sting site
Asthma exacerbation or other cause of acute bronchospasm
Angioedema of other cause (e.g. ACE-inhibitor related)
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis of anaphylaxis based on recognised criteria
Serial serum tryptase to support a diagnosis of mast cell activation
Specific IgE testing and skin testing to the relevant venom (after recovery, via allergy services)
In massive envenomation: full blood count, haemolysis markers, creatine kinase, renal and liver function
Electrocardiography and monitoring during and after severe reactions
redFlags: Airway compromise from laryngeal oedema or stridor
Rapid progression of symptoms after the sting
Massive multiple stings with evidence of haemolysis or organ injury
reference.prognosis: Anaphylaxis responds well to prompt adrenaline and supportive care, with full recovery expected, though delay increases mortality. Venom immunotherapy substantially reduces the risk of future systemic reactions; massive envenomation carries a higher risk of organ injury.
pitfalls: Delaying intramuscular adrenaline while giving antihistamines or steroids first
Discharging without observation for a possible biphasic reaction
Failing to prescribe an adrenaline auto-injector and refer for allergy assessment
Mistaking the toxic syndrome of massive envenomation for simple allergy and missing haemolysis or rhabdomyolysis
references: International anaphylaxis and insect venom allergy guidelines
management: Prompt intramuscular adrenaline as the first-line, life-saving treatment for anaphylaxis, repeated as needed and never delayed for other agents
Supportive resuscitation with high-flow oxygen, airway support, supine positioning, and intravenous fluids for distributive shock, with antihistamines and corticosteroids as adjuncts
Rapid removal of any retained stinger to halt ongoing venom delivery
A period of observation after apparent recovery to detect biphasic reactions
Discharge with adrenaline auto-injectors, training in their use, a personalised emergency action plan, and sting-avoidance advice
Referral to allergy services for specific IgE and skin testing and venom immunotherapy, which markedly reduces the risk of future systemic reactions
Supportive management of massive envenomation with monitoring and treatment of haemolysis, rhabdomyolysis, and renal or hepatic injury
